newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Asian steam coal market seen rising.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Asian steam coal market seen rising.

text.p: Asia's steam coal trade will jump by more than 100 million tonnes to 300 million tonnes in 2010, Haruo Tsuchida, executive managing director of Japan's biggest power group, the Electric Power Development Co, Ltd (EPDC), said on Tuesday.

In a speech prepared for a Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) forum coal conference here, Tsuchida said Asia's steam coal market was expected to grow by about 60 million tonnes to slightly less than 200 million tonnes in year 2000.

Traditional markets such as Japan, Korea, Taiwan and Hong Kong would continue to grow steadily, but their share of growth to year 2010 would dip to about one-third from a share of more than half from 1996 to year 2000, he said.
Emerging markets, such as ASEAN (Association of Southeast Asian Nations) members, China and India were expected to show substantially higher growth in steam coal imports, he said.
But Tsuchida said that on the brink of this boom, coal producers faced some dangers, particularly the ability of emerging markets to pay and the possibility that prices could fall.
"Major uncertainty exists as to how to finance the considerable expansion of electricity generation capacity required," he said.
Future development of the emerging markets depended on independent power producer (IPP) projects.
But few had reached the construction stage so far because of a need for an improved business environment with laws and legislation, he said.
He also saw conservative IPP requirements of financiers and governments as an impediment to stable fuel supply.
"Some IPPs seek to introduce into long-term contracts (written to protect against supply shortages) pricing systems which stabilise coal prices in the medium to long-term," he said.
"There may be some contracts with IPPs where the price of coal is rigidly set below the market porice," he said. This would provide little incentive to coal supply expansion.
This year had already shown a shift by Japan toward greater use of spot steam coal purchases, he said.
This reflected both a policy change toward lowest cost buying as well as Japan's move away from benchmark pricing in the Australia-Japan coking coal round of last year, he said.
Japanese buyers last year moved coal pricing negotiations onto a mine-by-mine basis, further dividing sellers.

The 1990s had shifted toward lowest-cost coal purchase strategies from the 1980s, which concentrated on a mixture of cost and supply security, which in turn had shifted from the 1970s when Japan used coal to diversify away from high-priced OPEC oil, Tsuchida noted.

The chief of Japan's biggest, state-owned power utility chain said that despite the shift in growth toward emerging markets, Japanese power utilities were still projected to double their steam coal requirements over the decade to Japanese fiscal year 2005, to 70 million tonnes.
The EPDC would procure an additional 10 million tonnes of imported coal in year 2010, against its current annual requirement of seven million tonnes, he said.
The EPDC planned to invest in a further coal mine expansion in Queensland, beyond its existing investment in the big Blair Athol mine, he said but did not elaborate.
Asia's increased electricity generation capacity over this period was expected to be 666 GW, with China, East Asia and Southeast Asia accounting for 276 GW, 252 GW and 138 GW respectively, he said.
About half of new power generation plants to begin operation by year 2010 were expected to be coal-fired, he said.
-- Sydney Newsroom 61-2 9373-1800
